record.paper_title: Towards Knowledge Exchange: State-of-the-Art and Open Problems
record.original_question: How can knowledge-base mapping generation tools scale to large source and target knowledge bases by using methods more sophisticated than simple slicing, such as modularization or partitioning, while still generating mapping rules efficiently?

evidence.quote: One of the most important challenges that KMGTs face is the scale of the KBs. Kensho uses a simple method for slicing the KBs in order to be able to deal with larger scale source and target [34]. However, more sophisticated methods such as modularization [36,45,70] or partitioning [38,67,69] can be adopted to help in efficient generation of mapping rules when dealing with large scale KBs.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let a knowledge base (KB) be a pair $K = (S, A)$ where $S$ is a schema (a finite set of classes and properties with subclass/subproperty relations and domain/range constraints) and $A$ is a finite set of assertions over $S$. A mapping between two knowledge bases $K_1 = (S_1, A_1)$ and $K_2 = (S_2, A_2)$ is a finite set $M$ of mapping rules, each of the form $\varphi(\bar x) \rightsquigarrow \psi(\bar x)$, where $\varphi$ is a conjunctive query over $S_1$ and $\psi$ is a conjunctive query over $S_2$. A knowledge-base mapping generation tool (KMGT) is an algorithm that, given $K_1$ and $K_2$, outputs such a set $M$.

Consider the following scalability problem. Suppose $|S_1|, |S_2|, |A_1|, |A_2|$ are too large to be processed in memory by a direct KMGT. A simple slicing approach partitions each KB into disjoint chunks of bounded size and applies the KMGT independently to each pair of chunks; this can miss mapping rules that span chunks and can produce redundant or inconsistent rules.

Problem. Design a KMGT framework that scales to arbitrarily large source and target knowledge bases by using either
(i) modularization, in which each KB is decomposed into a family of modules $\{M_i\}$ such that for every signature $\Sigma$ of interest there exists a module $M_i$ that is a conservative extension of the relevant fragment of the KB with respect to $\Sigma$; or
(ii) partitioning, in which each KB is split into possibly overlapping parts according to a structural or semantic criterion (e.g., graph cuts on the schema graph, clustering of assertions, or locality-based partitions).

Specifically, give an algorithm together with a formal correctness and efficiency analysis establishing:
(a) Soundness: every rule produced is logically entailed by the full KBs.
(b) Completeness (relative to a specified mapping language): every rule that a non-scalable reference KMGT would produce on the entire KBs is recovered, up to logical equivalence.
(c) Scalability: the total running time and memory are sub-linear in a meaningful parameter (e.g., polynomial in the largest module/partition size and near-linear in the total KB size), strictly improving upon simple slicing.

Either exhibit such an algorithm with proofs of (a)–(c), or prove an impossibility result identifying intrinsic obstacles (e.g., that no modularization/partitioning scheme of bounded module size can preserve completeness for a given mapping language).
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research challenge regarding scalability of knowledge-base mapping generation tools. No definitive scalable solution with formal soundness/completeness/efficiency guarantees based on modularization or partitioning appears to be established in the literature; ontology modularization and partitioning techniques exist but have not been shown to fully resolve the scalable mapping-generation problem.

status_evidence.title: Towards Knowledge Exchange: State-of-the-Art and Open Problems
status_evidence.snippet: More sophisticated methods such as modularization or partitioning can be adopted to help in efficient generation of mapping rules when dealing with large scale KBs.
status_evidence.claim: The problem of scaling KMGTs via modularization or partitioning is posed as open.
